overview: Ornithomimus edmontonicus was an ostrich-sized ornithomimosaur from the Late Cretaceous Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, about 68 million years ago. Exceptional specimens from the Dinosaur Park Formation preserve integument showing that adults were feathered on the arms (wing-like feathers) while their bodies bore scales, a pattern strikingly similar to modern ratite birds.

Ornithomimus is one of the best-documented North American ornithomimosaurs, known from multiple complete specimens spanning different growth stages. The arm-feather pattern in adults may have been used for brooding or display, paralleling the functional role of wing feathers in modern ostriches and emus.

fossilSites.name: Horseshoe Canyon Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Campanian to early Maastrichtian deposits preserving multiple Ornithomimus specimens including feathered examples.

fossilSites.name: Dinosaur Park Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian-aged beds yielding ornithomimosaur material alongside Parasaurolophus, ceratopsids and tyrannosaurids.

articles.title: Discovery and feather evidence
articles.body: Named by Marsh in 1890, Ornithomimus became better known through Lambe's Early 20th-century work on Alberta material. The feathered specimens described by van der Reest and colleagues in 2016 were the first direct evidence of integument in ornithomimosaurs and revealed a striking age-related pattern: juveniles lacked arm feathers; adults bore them. This mirrors the ontogenetic changes in modern ratites.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: Like all ornithomimosaurs, Ornithomimus had a small head, large eyes, a toothless beak, long arms with three subequal fingers, and long gracile hindlimbs. The metatarsal proportions are among the most bird-like of any non-avian dinosaur. There is evidence of a keratinous beak sheath.

articles.title: Diet and ecology
articles.body: The toothless beak and arm musculature suggest omnivory or herbivory rather than active predation. Ornithomimus coexisted with Albertosaurus and Troodon in a coastal lowland environment of rivers, swamps and open ground. Its rapid locomotion would have been its primary defence against predators.

fossilRecord.formations: Dinosaur Park and Horseshoe Canyon formations, Canada
fossilRecord.material: Skeletons and feather-impression specimens referred to Ornithomimus.
fossilRecord.evidence: Long limbs, toothless jaws and feather traces support bird-like body covering in ornithomimosaurs.

record.description: Ornithomimus was an ostrich-like ornithomimid from western North America. The well-known species O. edmontonicus is represented by multiple skeletons, including specimens preserving feather impressions; the type species O. velox is far more fragmentary.
facts: Juvenile and adult specimens show down-like body feathers, with larger arm feathers in adults.
The edentulous beak is preserved, but herbivory, omnivory and filter-feeding proposals remain debated.
Genus-level ranges must distinguish O. edmontonicus from fragmentary O. velox and historical referrals.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure species records span late Campanian to early Maastrichtian formations; a range to 66 Ma relies on disputed referrals.
